notes: The image’s proportions are sixty cubits by six. A cubit is a length based on the forearm; the text does not specify a modern measurement or the image’s design.
The ancient instrument names are not all securely identified. The list in verse 7 is shorter than the lists in verses 5, 10, and 15; the translation preserves that difference.
The traditional read form has “your god” in the singular; the written form is plural. The full source record preserves both.

The opening Aramaic condition is difficult: it may concern the situation or God’s ability to deliver. The following “even if not” leaves the outcome of rescue open while affirming the speakers’ refusal to worship the image.
“A son of the gods” is the king’s description of the fourth figure. In verse 28 he speaks of God’s angel. The translation does not insert an identification absent from his words.
vocabulary: A heated enclosure used here as a means of execution.
Here, the accusers associated with the Babylonian court.

notes: These verses are numbered 3:31–33 in the pinned Aramaic source. The following verses of this chapter are numbered 4:1–34 there.
“Spirit of the holy gods” preserves the king’s religious language. The Aramaic can also be understood as referring to the holy God; the speaker’s wording is not a new statement by the narrator.
The “watcher” is a heavenly figure. “Seven times” does not itself specify years.
The Aramaic verb can convey breaking off or redeeming. The advice links righteous action with mercy to the poor; it does not explain a system for purchasing forgiveness.
“Father” and “son” can describe ancestral or dynastic relationships. The translation preserves the narrative’s terms without constructing a genealogy.
The Aramaic says that the bonds of his loins loosened. It depicts bodily terror; interpretations include collapse of strength and loss of bodily control.
“Third ruler” is a possible reading of an unusual title; “one of three rulers” is another. The verse does not explain a co-regency.
The words of the inscription evoke counting, weighing, and dividing. “Peres,” the singular form corresponding to “Upharsin,” also sounds like the name Persia.
This verse is 6:1 in the pinned source. Darius the Mede’s identity is not explained here; his age is given as about sixty-two.
vocabulary: Containers and utensils used in worship.
A word associated with weighing; the interpretation says the king has been found deficient.

notes: The king’s words may be read as a wish, “May your God rescue you,” or as confidence that God will rescue Daniel.
The Aramaic term rendered “diversions” is uncertain. It describes something normally brought to the king that he did without that night.
The account explicitly includes the accusers’ wives and children in the execution. Retaining that detail does not turn the king’s action into an instruction for readers.
The verse names Darius and Cyrus without explaining their relationship. This draft does not identify them as the same person.
“Like a son of man” describes a humanlike figure in contrast to the beasts. The figure comes toward the Ancient of Days; the scene does not describe descent to earth.

“Holy ones” can refer to heavenly beings or to a people belonging to God; the vision connects them without fully explaining the relationship. Verse 22 may mean judgment in their favor or authority to judge given to them.
“A time, times, and half a time” is retained as an expression, without a calendar calculation. The pronoun “they” can be related to the holy ones or to the preceding times and law.
The final singular “his” and “him” can be understood of the Most High or in relation to the collective people. The translation preserves the pronouns.
vocabulary: The vision’s title for the venerable figure seated in judgment.
Here explained as kings; the image conveys power.

notes: The source returns to Hebrew in this chapter after the Aramaic section ending at 7:28.
“One of them” may refer to the horns or to the winds/directions mentioned immediately before. The draft leaves the reference open.

The Hebrew is compressed and its pronouns are difficult. “Regular offering” supplies the understood sacrificial practice; “set right” can include the sanctuary’s restoration and vindication. The 2,300 evenings and mornings are not converted into a different total.
The final phrase may mean that no one understood the vision or that Daniel did not understand it. His distress is clear; its resolution is not supplied.
vocabulary: The two kingdoms explicitly named in the interpretation of the ram.
The kingdom explicitly named in the interpretation of the goat; the first king remains unnamed in the verse.

notes: The pinned Hebrew has “for the Lord’s sake,” in the third person. The wording has not been silently changed to “for your sake, Lord.”
The phrase about Gabriel’s movement is difficult; it is commonly understood as swift flight, but weariness has also been proposed. The evening offering supplies the time reference.

“Sevens” names units of seven without adding “years” to the verse. “A most holy place” renders a phrase that can designate a most holy thing or place; some understand a person. The written/read record also preserves a difference involving sealing or ending sin.

The draft follows the source’s strong pause after seven sevens, then speaks of sixty-two sevens. The anointed figures and later “he” are not named. “Wing of abominations” and the final object of devastation are difficult; no single historical or future chronology is inserted into the translation.
vocabulary: Deal with guilt so that the damaged relationship can be restored; the verse does not explain the mechanism.
Someone set apart for a role; the phrase itself is not a personal name.

notes: The Hebrew term for “conflict” can also describe warfare or strenuous service. It introduces the weight of the vision without specifying a modern event.
Uphaz is the name in the pinned text. It has not been changed to Ophir.
The pinned wording says the speaker remained beside the kings of Persia. It differs from readings that say he left Michael there.
vocabulary: In this vision, a figure associated with a people or kingdom, including Persia and Israel.
The vision’s designation for what is written concerning the events being disclosed.

notes: The speaker continues from chapter 10. The pronoun “him” is not fully explained; Darius or Michael may be in view.
The alliances are described through royal daughters. Several pronouns are difficult; the translation clarifies the narrative where supported but does not supply the rulers’ names.

“Splendor of the kingdom” is an obscure phrase. The army’s “sweeping away” in verse 26 is also difficult; the verb can describe overflowing. These lines remain provisional readings of the pinned Hebrew.
Kittim is retained as a geographical name. “The desire of women” is not explained in the text and should not be silently turned into a claim about sexuality or a particular deity.

The recognition clause in verse 39 and the changing pronouns in verse 40 are uncertain. Verse 45 has “seas” in the plural. The draft does not fill in a detailed identification of the unnamed final ruler.
vocabulary: A profaning presence or practice associated here with removal of the regular offering.
Those who understand and teach others; understanding does not spare them suffering in this account.

notes: The source says “many,” and describes waking to two enduring outcomes. The translation does not replace that wording with a comprehensive scheme of resurrection.
The expressions “a time, times, and half a time,” 1,290 days, and 1,335 days are preserved separately. The text’s figures are not harmonized into one calculation.
Daniel is told to rest and then stand in his allotted place at the end of the days. The wording leaves the manner of that fulfillment unstated.
vocabulary: The great prince described as standing over Daniel’s people.
Secure a document or vision; the command concerns its preservation until the stated time.
